lines.text:
Spin, Rinse, Repeat — A Visit to the Laundromat

A laundromat is a self-service laundry — a public space where customers wash and dry their own clothes using coin-operated or card-operated machines. For students, travellers, and anyone without a washing machine at home, it is a weekly necessity. It is also an excellent classroom for practical vocabulary.

The machines divide into two types. A washing machine cleans clothes. A dryer removes moisture with heat. Washing machines come as front loaders — with a door on the front — or top loaders — with a lid on top. The wash cycle involves several stages: the machine fills with water, agitates the clothes with detergent, drains, and then enters the spin cycle to extract water. A rinse stage removes soap residue. The tumble dry cycle in the dryer rotates clothes in heated air.

Operating a machine requires preparation. A coin slot or a card reader accepts payment. A start button begins the cycle. A timer displays the remaining minutes. The customer must first sort their laundry — separating whites, darks, and colours to prevent dye transfer. Delicate fabrics — silk, wool — require gentler settings: cold wash, tumble dry low, or hang dry. Cotton and denim tolerate warm wash. Some items are labelled dry clean only, meaning they cannot be washed in water at all.

Laundry products are essential. Detergent cleans. Fabric softener reduces stiffness and adds fragrance. Bleach whitens whites — but destroys colours. A stain remover is applied directly to marks before washing. A dryer sheet reduces static in the dryer. A lint roller removes fibres from finished garments. A measuring cup ensures the correct amount of detergent.

Clothes themselves form a large vocabulary set: a shirt, pants, socks, underwear, a towel, a sheet, a blanket, a dress, a jacket, and jeans — each with its own care requirements. A label inside each garment provides washing instructions.

After drying, the customer moves to a folding table to fold clothes. A cart or a basket carries items between machines. Hangers hold shirts and dresses to prevent creasing. Clothespins secure items on a line for air drying. A mesh bag protects delicate items during the wash cycle. An iron removes wrinkles from cotton and linen.

The laundromat's shared spaces include a bench for waiting, a vending machine for purchasing detergent, a change machine for converting notes to coins, a clock for tracking time, a sign listing rules and prices, a floor drain for overflow, a lost and found for forgotten items, and a trash can.

The actions are sequential: sort, load, add detergent, select cycle, start, wait, unload, transfer to dryer, dry, fold, and leave. Pre-soaking treats stubborn stains. Stain treating targets specific marks. The process is simple, repetitive, and — for language learners — rich in everyday vocabulary that transfers directly to home laundry, travel, and shopping for cleaning products.

lines.text: Excuse me — I've never used one of these before. How do I start the washing machine?

lines.text: First, sort your clothes — darks, whites, delicates. Then load them into the drum. Don't overfill it.
lines.name: First, sort your clothes — darks, whites, delicates. Then load them into the drum. Don't overfill it.

lines.text: Got it. Where do I put the laundry detergent?

lines.text: In the detergent dispenser on top. You can add fabric softener in the second slot. Skip the bleach unless you're doing whites.
lines.name: In the detergent dispenser on top. You can add fabric softener in the second slot. Skip the bleach unless you're doing whites.

lines.text: How do I pay? I don't see a card reader.

lines.text: It's coin-operated — you need quarters for the coin slot. There's a change machine by the folding table.

lines.text: Which cycle should I choose? There are so many settings on the dial.

lines.text: For everyday clothes, use the normal cycle. Delicates need a gentle wash. Set the water temperature to warm — cold for darks.

lines.text: The machine is done. Now what — straight into the dryer?

lines.text: Check the lint trap first — clean it out or your clothes won't dry properly. Then choose medium heat and set the timer.

lines.text: The dryers are over there. Twenty minutes should be enough for a normal load. Check your labels first — some things shouldn't go in the dryer.

lines.text: 'Clothes' (/kloʊðz/) = garments you wear. 'Cloths' (/klɒθs/) = pieces of fabric (cleaning cloths, dishcloths). The spelling difference is small but the meaning is completely different. 'Clothes' is always plural — never *'a clothes.' Use 'a piece of clothing' or 'an item of clothing' for singular. 'Clothing' (uncountable) is the formal/general term.

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggest me to use). Correct: suggest + that-clause (subjunctive): 'suggested that I use.' Suggest + gerund: 'suggested using.' Same restriction: 'recommend', 'propose.' Compare: 'She advised me to use cold wash' — 'advise' DOES take object + infinitive.

lines.text: 'Jeans' is always plural: 'my jeans are', 'these jeans', 'them.' Use 'a pair of jeans' for singular reference: 'This pair of jeans is...' Same pattern: trousers, shorts, pants, tights, pyjamas — all plural nouns. 'I bought two pairs of jeans' (not *two jeans).

lines.text: 'Be used to' + gerund: 'used to washing' (accustomed). 'Used to' + infinitive: 'I used to wash' (past habit — I don't any more). 'Get used to' + gerund: 'getting used to washing.' The 'to' in 'be used to' is a preposition (takes -ing), not part of an infinitive. Three distinct structures — the form determines the meaning.

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer machines', 'fewer dryers', 'fewer coins.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less detergent', 'less time', 'less space.' Washing machines are countable individual items, so 'fewer' is correct. Quick test: if you can put a number before it ('three machines'), use 'fewer.'

lines.text: 'Laundrette' (BrE) = 'laundromat' (AmE). Both are self-service laundry shops. 'Laundry' can mean: the clothes to be washed ('I need to do the laundry'), the room where you wash ('the laundry room'), or the act of washing ('laundry day').

lines.text: Most British homes have a washing machine in the kitchen — this surprises many visitors. In American homes, the washer and dryer are usually in a separate utility room, basement, or garage. Shared laundry rooms are common in apartment buildings.

lines.text: UK/Europe: washing temperatures in Celsius (30°C, 40°C, 60°C). US: cold, warm, hot (no specific degrees shown). European machines typically use lower temperatures and longer cycles. American machines use more water but shorter cycles.

lines.text: A tub with a number = wash at that temperature. A triangle = bleach allowed. A square with a circle = tumble dry. An iron = ironing. A circle = dry clean. An X through any symbol = do not do this. These symbols are international but many people don't know them!
